facts.statement: Thalassodromeus was described by Kellner and Campos in 2002.
facts.quote: authority: Kellner & Campos, 2002

facts.statement: The original skull of Thalassodromeus was discovered in 1983 in the Araripe Basin of northeastern Brazil.
facts.quote: The original skull, discovered in 1983 in the Araripe Basin of northeastern Brazil, was collected in several pieces.

facts.statement: In 2002, Alexander Kellner and Diogenes de Almeida Campos designated the skull as the holotype for Thalassodromeus sethi.
facts.quote: In 2002, the skull was made the holotype specimen of Thalassodromeus sethi by palaeontologists Alexander Kellner and Diogenes de Almeida Campos.

facts.statement: Thalassodromeus had one of the largest known pterosaur skulls, measuring around 1.42 meters in length, and possessed one of the largest cranial crests of any vertebrate.
facts.quote: Thalassodromeus had one of the largest known skulls among pterosaurs, around 1.42 m long, with one of the proportionally largest cranial crests of any vertebrate.

facts.statement: Although only the skull is known, Thalassodromeus is estimated to have had a wingspan between 4.2 and 4.5 meters.
facts.quote: Though only the skull is known, the animal is estimated to have had a wingspan of 4.2 to 4.5 m.

facts.statement: Thalassodromeus had toothless jaws with sharp upper and lower edges.
facts.quote: The jaws were toothless, and had sharp upper and lower edges.

facts.statement: Thalassodromeus is known from the Romualdo Formation, where it coexisted with other pterosaurs, dinosaurs, and animals.
facts.quote: Thalassodromeus is known from the Romualdo Formation, where it coexisted with many other types of pterosaurs, dinosaurs and other animals.

facts.statement: Some scholars argue that the crest resembles the crown of the Egyptian god Amon rather than Seth.
facts.quote: Other scholars have pointed out that the crest was instead similar to the crown of Amon.

facts.statement: A species named T. sebesensis was described in 2015 based on a crest fragment, but it was later identified as part of a turtle shell.
facts.quote: Another species (T. sebesensis) was described in 2015 based on a supposed crest fragment, but this was later shown to be part of a turtle shell.

facts.statement: Thalassodromeus is grouped with Tupuxuara in the clade Thalassodromidae, which is placed either within Tapejaromorpha or Neoazhdarchia depending on the study.
facts.quote: The closest relative of Thalassodromeus was Tupuxuara; both are grouped in a clade called Thalassodromidae, which, depending on the study, has been placed either within Tapejaromorpha, closely related to the family Tapejaridae, or within Neoazhdarchia, closely related to the family Dsungaripteridae.

facts.statement: The first known specimen was collected in 1983 near Santana do Cariri in the Araripe Basin of northeastern Brazil.
facts.quote: The first known specimen of this pterosaur (an extinct order of flying reptiles) was collected in 1983 near the town of Santana do Cariri in the Araripe Basin of northeastern Brazil.

facts.statement: The skull was first reported in a 1984 Italian book and preliminarily described in 1990 by Kellner and Campos.
facts.quote: The skull was first reported in a 1984 Italian book, and preliminarily described and figured in 1990 by palaeontologists Alexander Kellner and Diogenes de Almeida Campos.

facts.statement: In 2015, Headden and Campos described the jaw tip as a new genus, Banguela oberlii, interpreting it as a dsungaripterid.
facts.quote: Palaeontologists Jaime A. Headden and Herbert B. N. Campos coined the new binomial Banguela oberlii, based on their reinterpretation of the jaw tip as belonging to a toothless member of the family Dsungaripteridae, in 2015.

facts.statement: In 2018, Pêgas, Costa, and Kellner reclassified B. oberlii as the species T. oberlii within Thalassodromeus.
facts.quote: In their 2018 re-description of the further-prepared T. sethi holotype skull, palaeontologists Rubi V. Pêgas, Fabiana R. Costa, and Kellner assigned B. oberlii back to Thalassodromeus while recognising it as a distinct species, and thereby created the new combination T. oberlii.

facts.statement: In 2025, Pinheiro and colleagues reaffirmed that T. oberlii belongs in Thalassodromeus.
facts.quote: The palaeontologist Felipe L. Pinheiro and colleagues reiterated that T. oberlii belonged in Thalassodromeus in 2025.

facts.statement: In 2015, Grellet-Tinner and Codrea named T. sebesensis based on a crest fragment found in Romania.
facts.quote: In 2015 palaeontologists Gerald Grellet Tinner and Vlad A. Codrea named a new species, T. sebesensis, based on what they interpreted as part of a cranial crest in a concretion found near the Sebeș River in Romania.

facts.statement: Dyke and colleagues rejected the identification of T. sebesensis as a pterosaur, arguing it was a fragment of the turtle Kallokibotion bajazidi.
facts.quote: Palaeontologist Gareth J. Dyke and a large team of colleagues immediately rejected the pterosaurian identification of the T. sebesensis fossil, instead arguing that it was a misidentified part of a plastron (lower shell) of the prehistoric turtle Kallokibotion bajazidi (named in 1923).

facts.statement: The entire skull of Thalassodromeus sethi is estimated to be 1.42 meters long.
facts.quote: The entire skull is estimated to have been 1.42 m long

facts.statement: Based on related pterosaurs, the wingspan of Thalassodromeus sethi was estimated to be between 4.2 and 4.5 meters.
facts.quote: Based on related pterosaurs, its wingspan was 4.2 to 4.5 m

facts.statement: The cranial crest of Thalassodromeus sethi varied in thickness from 1 to 10.5 millimeters.
facts.quote: The crest varied from 1 to 10.5 mm in thickness

facts.statement: Like all members of its clade, Thalassodromeus had toothless jaws.
facts.quote: As in all members of its clade, the jaws were edentulous (toothless)

facts.statement: The snout of Thalassodromeus sethi was 650 millimeters long from the tip of the premaxilla to the quadrate-articular joint.
facts.quote: The rostrum (snout) was 650 mm long from the tip of the premaxilla to the joint where the quadrate bone of the skull connected with the articular bone of the lower jaw

facts.statement: Although incomplete, the total length of the lower jaw of Thalassodromeus sethi is estimated at 670 millimeters.
facts.quote: Although the lower jaw of T. sethi is incomplete, its total length is estimated at 670 mm

facts.statement: The mandibular symphysis occupied 47 percent of the total length of the lower jaw.
facts.quote: 47 percent of which was occupied by the mandibular symphysis

facts.statement: The symphyseal shelf on the upper surface of the mandibular symphysis extended for 170 millimeters.
facts.quote: The symphyseal shelf, the upper surface of the symphysis, extended for 170 mm

facts.statement: It is debated whether the fossil T. oberlii represents a second species of Thalassodromeus or a different genus named Banguela.
facts.quote: the possible second species of Thalassodromeus, or possibly a different genus (Banguela) which is known only from a jaw tip

facts.statement: Kellner and Campos originally classified Thalassodromeus in the family Tapejaridae due to its large crest and large nasoantorbital fenestra.
facts.quote: Kellner and Campos originally assigned Thalassodromeus to the family Tapejaridae, based on its large crest and large nasoantorbital fenestra.

facts.statement: In 2006, Martill and Naish argued that Tapejaridae was a paraphyletic group and placed Thalassodromeus (within Tupuxuara) as the sister taxon to Azhdarchidae.
facts.quote: Martill and Naish considered Tapejaridae a paraphyletic (unnatural) group in 2006, and found Tupuxuara (which included Thalassodromeus in their analysis) to be the sister taxon to the family Azhdarchidae.

facts.statement: In 2007, Kellner and Campos defended the family Tapejaridae by splitting it into Tapejarinae and Thalassodrominae, the latter containing Thalassodromeus and Tupuxuara.
facts.quote: Kellner and Campos defended the validity of Tapejaridae in 2007, dividing it into two clades: Tapejarinae and Thalassodrominae, the latter containing Thalassodromeus (the type genus) and Tupuxuara.

facts.statement: Mark Witton elevated Thalassodrominae to the family level Thalassodromidae and placed it within the clade Neoazhdarchia.
facts.quote: Witton further converted the subfamily name Thalassodrominae into the family name Thalassodromidae, and considered the clade part of Neoazhdarchia.

facts.statement: A 2011 study by Pinheiro and colleagues supported grouping Tapejarinae and Thalassodrominae within the family Tapejaridae alongside Chaoyangopterinae.
facts.quote: A 2011 analysis by Pinheiro and colleagues upheld the grouping of the clades Tapejarinae and Thalassodrominae in the family Tapejaridae, joined by the Chaoyangopterinae.

facts.statement: In 2021, Cerqueira and colleagues identified the new genus Kariridraco as the sister taxon to Thalassodromeus and Tupuxuara.
facts.quote: In 2021, palaeontologist Gabriela M. Cerqueira and colleagues found their new genus Kariridraco to be the sister taxon of Thalassodromeus and Tupuxuara.

facts.statement: The classification of Thalassodromeus and its relatives remains one of the most contentious issues in pterosaur research.
facts.quote: The classification of Thalassodromeus and its closest relatives is one of the most contentious issues regarding their group.

facts.statement: The placement of the clade containing Thalassodromeus within Azhdarchoidea has been disputed, with researchers proposing different names like Thalassodrominae and Tupuxuaridae.
facts.quote: The interrelationship of these clades within the larger clade Azhdarchoidea remained disputed, and the clade containing Thalassodromeus and Tupuxuara had received different names from different researchers (Thalassodrominae and Tupuxuaridae).

facts.statement: Thalassodromeus shared a crest made primarily of bone with Tupuxuara, whereas other group members had crests with a large soft tissue component.
facts.quote: Kellner elaborated on the relationships within Tapejaridae in 2004, and pointed out that Thalassodromeus and Tupuxuara also shared a crest consisting primarily of bone; the crest had a large component of soft tissue in other members of the group.

facts.statement: The genus Thalassodromeus was named in 2002 by Alexander Kellner and Diogenes de Almeida Campos.
facts.quote: El género fue nombrado en 2002 por Alexander Kellner y Diogenes de Almeida Campos.

facts.statement: The holotype of Thalassodromeus is a damaged partial skull, DGM 1476-R, found in the Santana Formation.
facts.quote: El género está representado por el holotipo DGM 1476-R, un cráneo parcial dañado, hallado en la Formación Santana.

facts.statement: Thalassodromeus had pointed, toothless jaws.
facts.quote: Las mandíbulas acababan en punta y eran desdentadas.

facts.statement: Thalassodromeus had a wingspan of approximately 4.5 meters.

facts.statement: A referred lower jaw fragment, DGM 1476-M, indicates an even larger specimen with a wingspan of 5.3 meters.

facts.statement: Kellner hypothesized that Thalassodromeus fed similarly to the modern skimmer, dragging its lower jaw in the water while flying.
facts.quote: Kellner creyó que Thalassodromeus se alimentaba de forma muy similar al actual rayador; arrastrando su mandíbula inferior en el agua mientras volaba.

facts.statement: Subsequent research suggested that the jaw and neck anatomy made skimming the water in this manner unfeasible for Thalassodromeus and other large pterosaurs due to drag and high energy costs.
facts.quote: Sin embargo, la investigación posterior mostró que la anatomía de la mandíbula y el cuello sugerían que para este y otros grandes pterosaurios no era factible rozar el agua de esa manera debido al arrastre: el gasto de energía podría haber sido demasiado alto.

facts.statement: Kellner and Campos proposed that the crest could have been used for display, species recognition, and was sexually dimorphic.
facts.quote: Kellner and Campos posited that the crest could have had additional functions, such as display; aided by colour, it could have been used in species recognition, and could also have been a sexually dimorphic feature (differing according to sex), as has been proposed for Pteranodon.

facts.statement: Pêgas and colleagues argued that thermoregulation did not correlate with crest growth relative to body size, citing toucan bills as a counter-example where such structures serve multiple functions.
facts.quote: They did not think that thermoregulation correlated with crest growth relative to body size, since the bills of toucans (the largest of any modern birds) grow drastically out of proportion to body size and function as thermoregulatory structures, as well as facilitating feeding and social behaviour.
